forces: Two violins, two violas and two cellos
performers: Hollywood String Quartet (Felix Slatkin and Paul Shure, violins; Paul Robyn, viola; Eleanor Aller, cello); Alvin Dinkin, viola; Kurt Reher, cello
intro: Side 2 of the Hollywood String Quartet’s recording of Verklärte Nacht, Op. 4, for six players, covers bars 229–418. It begins with the D major section, in which the man accepts the woman and her child, and continues through the muted passages to the quiet close.

sections.label: A · Cellos enter in D major
sections.mNote: Violas and cellos begin the man’s reply.

sections.label: B · Muted strings and harmonics
sections.mNote: F♯ major; muted runs and harmonics.

sections.label: C · Violin and cello duet
sections.mNote: Earlier themes return across the six players.

sections.label: Coda · Opening walking theme in major
sections.mNote: The opening walking theme returns with the man’s theme

sections.label: Coda · High violin over moving inner strings
sections.mNote: The second violin plays continuous figures beneath sustained upper notes.

cues.title: Section in D major
cues.text: Violas and cellos play a broad chord of D major, marked Sehr breit und langsam — very broadly and slowly. The first cello then plays an expressive line. In Dehmel’s poem, the man accepts the child his companion is carrying.
cues.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), p. 26, bars 229–240; Schoenberg’s programme notes (1950), example 10. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Muted strings in F♯ major
cues.text: The strings put on mutes. Quick violin runs cross held harmonics, notes made by touching the strings lightly. The key is F♯ major; in his 1950 programme notes Schoenberg identified this passage with the beauty of the moonlight.
cues.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), p. 27, bars 249–250: six-sharp signature, mutes and harmonics. Schoenberg’s 1950 programme notes, example 11. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Schoenberg’s programme note, 1950
cues.text: In 1950 Schoenberg wrote that the sextet “does not illustrate any action or drama”. He described it as a portrayal of nature and an expression of human emotion, and said that heard in this way it “can make you forget the poem” that inspired it.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s 1950 programme note, printed on the Capitol LP sleeve (Internet Archive item lp_schoenberg-verklaerte-nacht-op-4-transfigu_the-hollywood-string-quartet) and in German in Stil und Gedanke, pp. 453–457, at https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: Duet for violin and cello
cues.text: A duet for violin and cello follows the muted passage. Earlier themes return around it with new accompaniments and are developed. Schoenberg described the duet and these returns in his programme notes of 1950, examples 12–16.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s programme notes (1950), examples 12–16, describe the violin–cello duet and the return and development of earlier themes. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter from Dehmel, 12 December 1912
cues.text: Dehmel wrote to Schoenberg on 12 December 1912 after hearing the sextet. He had meant to follow his poem through the music, but he soon forgot to and listened only to the six strings.
cues.evidence: Richard Dehmel to Schoenberg, 12 December 1912, quoted in Therese Muxeneder’s work essay. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: New themes after the duet
cues.text: After the climax of the duet, a new melody enters for what Schoenberg called the “warmth that flows from one of us into the other”. Earlier themes return in reworked form. A second new theme follows for the man’s resolve.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s 1950 programme note, examples 15 and 16, as printed on the Capitol LP sleeve (Internet Archive item lp_schoenberg-verklaerte-nacht-op-4-transfigu_the-hollywood-string-quartet) and in German at https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First Vienna performance
cues.text: In his 1950 programme note Schoenberg recalled that the sextet “was hissed and caused riots and fist fights” at its first Vienna performance. “But very soon it became very successful.”
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s 1950 programme note, closing paragraph, as printed on the Capitol LP sleeve (Internet Archive item lp_schoenberg-verklaerte-nacht-op-4-transfigu_the-hollywood-string-quartet) and in German at https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: Original sextet scoring
cues.text: Schoenberg later arranged Verklärte Nacht for string orchestra, adding double basses in 1917 and revising the arrangement in 1943. Here the original six players are kept, and each violin, viola and cello part is played by one person.
cues.evidence: Arnold Schönberg Center work essay distinguishes the original sextet from the 1917 and 1943 string-orchestra versions and identifies the added double-bass part. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: Second new theme, the man’s resolution
cues.text: In his 1950 programme note Schoenberg described a second new theme as the man’s “dignified resolution”. The warmth between them “will transfigure your child”, so that it becomes “my own”.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s 1950 programme note, example 16, as printed on the Capitol LP sleeve (Internet Archive item lp_schoenberg-verklaerte-nacht-op-4-transfigu_the-hollywood-string-quartet) and in German at https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Climax and coda
cues.text: An ascent leads to the climax, where the second half of the man’s theme returns. This is the broad D-major melody that opened this side, “a man whose generosity is as sublime as his love”. A long coda follows.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s 1950 programme note, examples 10 and 16 and the closing climax, as printed on the Capitol LP sleeve (Internet Archive item lp_schoenberg-verklaerte-nacht-op-4-transfigu_the-hollywood-string-quartet) and in German at https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, opening theme in major
cues.text: In the coda the opening walking theme returns in the major, set in counterpoint with the man’s theme, the principal theme of the fourth section. Dehmel’s final stanza returns to the night walk beneath the same moon.
cues.evidence: Therese Muxeneder’s work essay identifies the opening motif in major and the fourth section’s principal theme as its counterpoint in the coda; Dehmel’s final stanza returns to the night walk. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hollywood String Quartet recording, 1950
cues.text: Capitol’s sleeve called this the first recording of the original sextet version and said it “was prepared under the personal supervision of the composer.” The Hollywood String Quartet made it on 21 and 22 August 1950, joined by Alvin Dinkin and Kurt Reher.
cues.evidence: Capitol L-8118 sleeve text (Internet Archive item lp_schoenberg-verklaerte-nacht-op-4-transfigu_the-hollywood-string-quartet); session dates and players in the Arnold Schönberg Center audio archive, recording 47. https://archive.schoenberg.at/av/aufnahme.php?id_aufnahme=47&action=view

cues.title: Final bars in D major
cues.text: The first violin holds long notes above running figures in the second violin, with violas and cellos filling the space between them. At the soft close of the piece the inner parts keep moving until all six instruments come to rest on D major.
cues.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), pp. 50–51, bars 409–418: sustained first violin, running second violin and final D-major chord. https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/manuskripte.php?werke_id=420&id_quelle=1213&herkunft=allewerke
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Mutes after the pause
transitions.from: A · Cellos enter in D major
transitions.how: A ritardando and a fermata slow the sextet before the music reaches F♯ major. The violins then play muted runs, and the violas and cellos play harmonics. Before the join, the D-major passage is bowed.

transitions.title: Duet for violin and cello
transitions.how: Above the accompaniment, a new melody develops into a duet for violin and cello. Schoenberg gives the longer phrases to the two instruments, and the remaining strings keep the accompaniment moving.
transitions.evidence: Schoenberg’s programme notes (1950), examples 12–14, describe the accompaniment and violin–cello duet. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

transitions.title: The opening walking motif returns
transitions.to: Coda · Opening walking theme in major
transitions.how: In the coda the opening walking motif returns in the major and is combined with the man’s answering melody. The six strings bring back phrases from both halves of the piece in the closing pages.
transitions.evidence: Therese Muxeneder’s account of the fifth section and Schoenberg’s programme notes (1950), final paragraph. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

transitions.title: Second violin figures continue to the close
transitions.from: Coda · Opening walking theme in major
transitions.to: Coda · High violin over moving inner strings
transitions.how: The first violin plays long notes above rapid figures in the second violin. Viola and cello parts, marked quiet, fill out the harmony. On the last page harmonics return briefly, and the running figures stop on the held D-major chord.

source.title: Schoenberg, Verklärte Nacht, original sextet score, Dreililien-Verlag, plate 345 (1905), composer’s copy E1
source.locator: Pages 26–27, 44–45 and 50–51, bars 229–418. Two violins, two violas and two cellos; the viola and cello pairs are grouped together here.

timeline.note: Violas and cellos open the D-major answer; the first cello plays the broad melody.
The violins join the lower strings and extend the man’s D-major answer.
Muted violins play runs over harmonics in the violas and cellos.
A duet for violin and cello grows out of the moving accompaniment, and earlier phrases pass among the six players.
The closing pages combine the walking theme in major with the man’s answering melody.
The first violin holds long notes above the second violin’s rapid figures, towards the final D-major chord.

composer.epithet: Composer who abandoned tonality, continued to study Bach and Brahms, and wrote a minuet using all twelve notes.
facts: Largely self-taught; lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky
Alban Berg and Anton Webern from 1904; later Hanns Eisler and John Cage
Prussian Academy of Arts, Berlin, 1926–33; UCLA, 1936–44
Painter; author of Harmonielehre (1911); founder of the Society for Private Musical Performances
composer.background:
At the première of Pierrot lunaire in Berlin on 16 October 1912, Albertine Zehme stood onstage in a Pierrot costume. Behind a screen, five instrumentalists watched Arnold Schoenberg conduct. They had held twenty-five ensemble rehearsals to prepare thirty-odd minutes of music in which the voice slid away from its written notes, the flautist also played piccolo and the violinist also played viola.

Schoenberg was born in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt in 1874 and began learning the violin as a child. His father died when he was fifteen. From 1891 to 1895 he worked in a bank, making music with friends and teaching himself from scores. Alexander Zemlinsky, whom he met through the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia, gave him lessons. From Brahms he learnt how a small phrase could grow through continual change, and from Wagner how long the resolution of a chord could be delayed.
